subsubtopic: PROPOSED REFERENCE OF CIDA EXPENDITURES AND ALLOCATIONS TO STANDING COMMITTEE-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Recent reports both within and outside of this House indicate that CIDA, the Canadian International Development Agency, is presently embarked on a $117 million capital expenditure program designed to facilitate the elimination of a budgetary surplus for the current fiscal year. This surplus, constituting as it does 16 per cent of the agency's $733 million approved expenditure for 1974-75, engenders the clear possibility of fiscal mismanagement or irregularity. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens):
That this House request forthwith an examination and scrutiny of budgetary expenditures and allocations for 1974-75 of the Canadian International Development Agency by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.

speechtext:

This matter concerns the recent ban on the transport of certain types of dangerous cargo on United States airlines. In view of the fact that Canadian airline pilots have expressed the fear that as a result of this ban dangerous and radioactive cargo may be transrouted through Canada on Canadian airlines under improper labelling, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Okanagan-Kootenay (Mr. Johnston):
That the government act immediately to upgrade its surveillance of air freight to control or prevent the shipment of cargo that endangers the life and safety of the public and airlines personnel.

speakeroldname: Miss Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us must be judged as one of the significant measures designed to implement the government's budget proposals announced last November 18. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has declared that the essential objective of the budget is to deal with the twin problems of inflation and slow growth, and he has certainly pinpointed the problem. In an extraordinary feat once believed impossible by economists, the Canadian government has managed to achieve both high inflation and rising unemployment simultaneously. This has the appearance of an apparent paradox but its effects are real enough. Nowhere is this more evident than in the field of housing. Figures released last week by Statistics Canada show that the price of a new house rose by over 80 per cent in many major Canadian cities in the last three years, yet at the same time housing starts were down 18 per cent last
Income Tax
year, from 1973, and starts in urban areas last December were 46 per cent lower than in December, 1973.
This great reduction in housing starts means that acute housing shortages will be experienced in Canadian cities throughout the whole of 1975 and well into 1976. The Canadian Conference Board predicts we will achieve only 180,000 starts this year, compared with 268,000 two years ago. What has the government done? The Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) seems oblivious to the crisis proportions of this situation, since his only response so far has been to revise his departmental objectives down to the 210,000 level, a target he considers within the realm of possibility. This is in spite of the fact that the Economic Council of Canada estimates that Canada needs to build at least 250,000 new houses a year from now to 1981 to meet the demands of a growing population.
The minister must be aware of the emphatic statement by the provincial housing ministers yesterday that 260,000 new homes must be built next year to meet the current need. They declared that the initiative in this area must come from the federal government. A slump of this magnitude in the residential construction industry has disastrous consequences for all other sectors of the economy. It directly relates to the lumber, textile, furniture and other ancillary industries. We have seen the tragic repercussions, socially and economically, in other areas as a result of the slowdown in construction. This has led to disruption and dislocation, slowdowns and lay-offs in other sectors of the economy.
Because the construction industry is highly labourintensive, the slump has fed rising unemployment, with a resultant lowering of income and expenditure. This multiplier effect has had a dampening impact on the rest of the economy. Housing has a major influence on capital flows. Construction contributes $21 billion to the gross national product, and with the current decline in this industry there is less growth in the economy, less productivity, less employment, less consumer spending. The situation is serious, yet the proposals in this budget and bill are completely inadequate to meet the problem.
We were presented with a budget in which every measure is a half measure, every step to stimulate the economy is a half step for fear of an inflation which the government refuses to tackle head on. The most charitable thing that can be said about the measures relating to housing in this bill is that they completely lack direction. To be less charitable, their goals are contradictory and the tools they employ are inefficient. Consider the goals. On the other hand, with the $500 grant for first-time home buyers, the opening up of the high ratio mortgage loans, the reduction of the building materials sales tax and the subsidies on mortgages, the government appears to be attempting to increase demand for housing; yet on the other hand, the registered home ownership savings plan provided for in this bill is aimed at deferring demand. In short, we have another ad hoc mixture of proposals working one against another with no clear direction.
Consider the $500 grant for first-time purchasers of new homes. This grant has severe limitations as the restric-

January 31, 1975
Income Tax
tions on the maximum housing price make it inaccessible to the majority of Canadians trying to purchase a home. Many, many Canadians have found this to be a discriminatory proposal since it applies to new housing only. The great majority of first-time buyers look to existing housing, which is normally less costly for this first purchase. The proposal motivates those persons better financially established to look to the higher-priced, newer homes. Incentives to continue this upward mobility would do much more to stimulate housing starts than trying to direct first-time purchasers to new homes. We urge the minister to consider seriously revising this proposal introduced last autumn to make it applicable to existing as well as to new homes.
AHOP has the same kind of restrictive measures and its lack of success is borne out by the number whose applications have been approved. There is no denying that there have been a great many applications but the approval rate is negligible. Take the figures for October 1974: 14 approvals in Halifax; 235 in Montreal; 42 in Hull; 52 in Regina; 32 in Vancouver; 14 in Winnipeg. But zero in Toronto; 7 in St. John's; 2 in Victoria; zero in Thunder Bay; zero in Kingston; zero in London; zero in Ottawa; zero in Moncton; zero in Oshawa; zero in Windsor. What I want to impress on the minister is that because of financial restrictions in these programs, they provide little or no impetus to the building industry.
The reduction of the sales tax on building material to 5 per cent was another half measure. Why was it not completely dropped, resulting in greater savings to the home buyer, more stimulation of the housing industry and, equally important, elimination of the elaborate and costly machinery required to collect that tax?
Just as the over-all goals of this budget are contradictory, so are the tools which it uses. Let us look at the carrying costs of land. There are several contradictions in the proposal, which eliminate the possibility of charging carrying costs on undeveloped land against other income for tax purposes. The Minister of Finance declared that both he and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs are persuaded that this measure will assist in bringing more land on to the market quickly to increase residential construction. But I am not nearly as persuaded as the minister. In fact, this kind of measure, by imposing an additional burden on the already severely strained requirements of many small builders for working capital, could force large numbers of them out of business.
The residential construction industry is now entering a period of severe economic distress. This provision will considerably exacerbate the existing liquidity problems, and while the large, well-financed development companies will undoubtedly survive, this measure could well force out of business many small builders who build the bulk of Canada's housing stock. In this case, the measure would have exactly the opposite effect of that sought by the minister, namely, it will decrease Canada's capacity to build homes just at the time when we need an increasing number of them.
Clearly, this provision should be applied in its present form only with regard to land speculators, and not with respect to land developers. This measure is particularly hard on small developers who make up about 90 per cent
[Miss MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands).;
of the market. Under this legislation, many of them will be penalized for delays in the development of land which are often caused by the lengthy processes involved in obtaining approval at the complex maze of municipal and provincial levels in servicing land and permitting development.
The second measure touched on in this bill and to be spelled out in regulation-that is, the proposed tax shelter with respect to apartment construction-is also a model of inefficiency. In the words of the Minister for Urban Affairs himself, the measure whereby capital cost allowances on rental construction can be charged against income from other sources is designed to "provide a quick and strong incentive to the construction of new rental housing units." That is an admirable goal, but this is a very ineffective tool with which to achieve it. This tax shelter is proposed to apply only to new, multiple-unit residential buildings begun before December 31, 1975. Unless a builder is virtually ready to proceed now with a building planned and already cleared through municipal and provincial authorities, it is unlikely that the building will be under construction by the end of 1975. It is not unusual for municipal and provincial building clearances to take up to two years. Far from encouraging the construction of new units, the timing of this proposal is such that it will barely apply to projects already under way. To be meaningful, this provision should apply for a much longer term.
On the whole, the provisions in clause 100 of this bill to set up the registered home ownership savings plan must be viewed as a step in the right direction. They set a good precedent of making tax deductions available for young couples to offset the cost of buying a home, but the plan in many ways is badly drafted. The thrust of the program is to discourage people from purchasing a home for some time; hence it will have a negative effect on the housing industry in the short term. The crisis is upon us now: we cannot wait for three, four or five years to tackle it.
Secondly, according to the legislation, the deadline for beginning such a plan this year would be March 1, just over a month away, yet it is unlikely that the government will be able to examine and approve the plans which each bank and trust company may have for implementing this bill, in time for many people to deposit their $1,000 before March 1. I hope that the government and the minister will take this into account and extend the deadline past March 1 this year. I want to make it clear, however, that we view the plan as only the barest beginning of the series of steps which should be taken to assist moderate and low-income groups to buy their own homes. A much more effective measure, and one this government could well afford, would be to make municipal taxes and a portion of mortgage payments tax deductible for those families whose income is low enough that they are spending more than 25 per cent of it, the accepted standard, on shelter costs. This is where the government should be directing its attention. Instead, we have in this bill piecemeal measures without clear direction and without the strength adequately to stimulate the housing market. It looks more like a public relations gesture than an economic program.
January 31, 1975

The government appears oblivious to the fact that the problems in the supply and demand aspect of the housing industry are caused by high interest rates and a subsequent shortage of mortgage money. Until direct measures are taken to reduce current mortgage rates and to make mortgage money available, housing starts will continue to decline and housing will continue to be priced beyond the means of many thousands of Canadian families. Moreover, by restricting AHOP and other programs exclusively to the buyers of new homes, the government has completely ignored the many families who can afford to buy only an older house. They have done virtually nothing to ease the impact of inflation on existing home owners. The proportion of public housing in this country remains at 2 per cent, one of the lowest in the western world, and there is little or nothing in this budget to ease the impact of inflation on the shelter costs of low and middle-income earners.
Instead, once again the Minister of Finance is using residential construction as a convenient safety-valve through which to manipulate the level of investment in the economy. Instead of co-ordinating residential construction through an over-all plan for housing, the government has put together another series of ad hoc measures which from time to time it calls a housing policy. Both the Economic Council of Canada and the Canadian Council on Social Development have warned against this approach. By stimulating demand for housing in fits and starts, the government simply makes an already volatile industry more unstable and unnecessarily raises the price of houses, which becomes increasingly difficult to reduce.
It is time the Canadian government developed an overall policy for housing which would guarantee consistent and continuous growth over the long term in that sector. Many economists, including John Kenneth Galbraith, have pointed out that the greatest concern of industry today is not so much immediate profits as stable growth over the long run. To achieve this there must be a certain consistency and regularity of investment in each sector of the economy, and there must be a certain predictability about where and how the government intends to encourage investment. To date we have had no such consistency from this government; we have had no over-all plan. This is particularly grave in the area of housing, where what is being affected by this ad hoc series of government policies is the basic need of Canadian families for shelter.
An emphatic condemnation of the housing policies of this bill and this budget comes from Professor T. A. Wilson, who is director of the Institute for Policy Analysis at the University of Toronto. If these are not credentials enough, he is also a member of the famous group of seven economists who personally advise the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on economic matters. Professor Wilson estimated that investment in residential construction would be down by over 17 per cent in 1975. Then, after careful examination, he estimates that these budget measures will change that figure by only 1.23 per cent-a negligible amount-for a total decline this year of over 16 per cent in residential construction. The need is already great and this is bad news for the Canadian economy and for the thousands of Canadian families who will be seeking homes and apartments this year.

I urge the minister to re-examine the restrictive measures he proposes to ease the crisis in the construction industry, and to recognize the critical demand for stimulus to housing starts, particularly for people in the lower and middle-income brackets. If my plea is not sufficient, I would urge the minister to pay attention to the remarks of his colleague, the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, yesterday when he stated that the biggest problem he has to face is the government spending priorities established in cabinet. I would urge, indeed I would plead with the Minister of Finance to rearrange those priorities so that housing is placed at the top.

Mr. Speaker, we have just listened to a very learned speech ably presented by the lady member of the opposition. I think all hon. members would agree with me, particularly the male members, that it is unfortunate that we do not have more ladies in the House of Commons. Today, in speaking to this bill, I would like to deal with a question which was very ably dealt with last night by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). It was also dealt with by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman). I speak of the question of tax policy as it affects the exploration and development of crude petroleum and natural gas and security of supply for Canada. At the outset I would say that we are in a very fortunate position in Canada. We are one of the few nations in the world, if not the only one, that is self-sufficient in crude petroleum and natural gas. Not only does this guarantee us a fairly high standard of living, but it enables us to speak in various groups and conferences, in confrontations with our neighbours and people who are not so neighbourly, in a way that will maintain the economic welfare of the nation and also guarantee peace and security.
Mr. Speaker, it was my good fortune recently to attend a NATO conference in Europe with members of the Conservative Party and the Liberal Party. We all came away with the impression that the supply of crude petroleum, which today is the main economic thrust in the western world, is more important in the world than armaments. Fifteen countries were represented at the NATO parliamentary session which met in London. We then proceeded to Lahr and Baden-Baden in Germany where Canadian troops are stationed. At the parliamentary sessions in London and in Germany, the Canadian members of parliament, of which I was one, together with the delegates of other nations, were briefed on the economic, political and defence positions of the western nations and, indeed, the economic, political and defence positions of the communist bloc nations.
The point I wish to make is that the question of energy supply and energy security was the main subject discussed. It was really the main thrust in reference to the economic and political welfare of the western world and its ability to continue to create and maintain the image of strength which has been the major factor in its ability to negotiate world problems and avoid a third world conflict which would certainly spell the destruction of our civilization. Security of supply of energy is so important to this

January 31, 1975
Income Tax
point that the tax policy of this nation in the very near future will determine whether we shall continue to have adequate supply and to be the only nation in the western world to be self-sufficient in energy.
The most important decision the cabinet of Canada has made in the last few years, in my opinion, is the decision to retreat from the hard position they took on taxing resource companies. As a result of that initial decision, exploration and development was brought to a halt. Geologists and economists predict that by 1980 Canada might be dependent on the Arab nations for oil. They are now charging $10 and $12 a barrel for petroleum, while western Canada receives only $6.50 either in the domestic market or the export market.
I want to direct my few words today to the question of security of supply of energy, its importance and its guarantee of economic health for Canada. The balance of power in the world no longer depends on armaments alone; energy has become equally important as the main factor in determining whether we are going to have war or peace, depression or prosperity. In the United States right now there is not only a recession in most states but a depression. We are doing better in Canada because of our self-sufficiency in energy. In passing, I might mention that the third dominant factor about to emerge is food supply and its availability. However, time does not permit me to go into this third factor today.
Economists point out that under the present tax structure it costs the producer in Saskatchewan 7 cents a barrel to produce oil. I do not know whether this is correct, but I have been advised that the pumps move slowly in Saskatchewan in the hope that some day this policy will be revised or the government will be defeated and we will have a reasonable and sane tax position that will encourage production, exploration and development.
The indictment against the Trudeau administration and some provincial governments will be that in 1974 and 1975 their leadership lacked the vision to see that Canada's prosperity had resulted in our being one of the few nations in the world that is self-sufficient in energy; that is, self-sufficient in oil and natural gas. We have been self-sufficient for a number of years because our resource corporations have had enough cash flow to explore and develop the petroleum industry. The indictment will be that the Trudeau government, for the purpose of purchasing votes, for pride, or for just plain cussedness, planned a tax policy to drive the capital flow, the personnel with know-how, the technology, the tools and equipment out of Canada to explore and develop petroleum elsewhere, leaving us in a situation where we must now live on our proven reserves until they run out.
This tax policy must be brought to an end. I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in reference to the Syncrude project, but I say it is discriminatory and that a policy must be brought in to cover all companies engaged in exploration and development to include not only the tar sands but also the finding of oil by the orthodox method of drilling. If we want to assure that corporations shall use their profits for development and exploration, surely rules and regulations could be incorporated into the tax structure to make sure that they do not put the profits in their jeans, as it were, but for further

exploration and development. This federal tax policy must be abandoned.
The three men who must take responsibility at the federal level for this lack of vision are the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald). The latter two may be Trudeau's puppets, but whatever they are they are going along with a policy that in the very near future will wreck the economy of this nation. No wonder the Minister of Finance is thinking of quitting and going to the World Bank. Security of supply of energy in the western world does not only promote peace but also economic stability. Canada faces a major depression if this tax resource policy is not abandoned.
The confrontation between the provinces and the federal government on the right to tax, the right to gouge the resource cash flow, has driven out drilling rigs, technical know-how, personnel and capital so that exploration and development are quickly coming to a standstill.
I have a clipping here from the Financial Post of November 30, 1974, which confirms what I say. Time does not permit me to read all of it, but the headline is pretty explicit:
Wind-down begins for frustrated oil industry
The article begins:
The Canadian oil industry, one of the fundamental economic forces in the country, seems about to blow its gasket.
The pressure on the industry became critical last week with the federal budget decision to disallow provincial oil royalties as deductions in figuring federal income tax-double taxation, in effect.
This was followed on the same day by a defiant constitutional battle-cry-
It goes on to point out that 96 per cent of the drilling rigs-and the companies are owned by Canadians-have left Canada to go to the United States, the North Sea and elsewhere to drill for oil. This will leave us in the position that in the very near future we will have to import oil from other areas. One of the most striking articles on this subject appeared in Time magazine on January 6 this year. Mr. Speaker, I do not know what my friend behind the curtains said just now, but whatever it was does not matter. This is too serious a problem for me to digress. This is the financial situation in which we find ourselves. The article in Time reads:

Moreover, Saudi Arabia's new wealth is simply the most spectacular symbol of the rising fortunes of the OPEC nations.
The oil cartel, composed of oil producing nations, is gouging industrialized nations to such an extent that Britain, France, the United States, Japan and Italy are heading for a slump. I continue reading from this article:
With their surplus of some $60 billion last year, they took in $164 million more each day and $6.8 million more each hour than, by best estimates, they can currently spend. At that rate of accumulation, the "Economist" of London calculates, OPEC could buy out all companies on the world's major stock exchanges in 15.6 years (at present quotations), all companies on the New York stock exchange in 9.2 years, all central banks' gold (at $170 an ounce) in 3.2 years, all U.S. direct investments abroad in 1.8 years, all companies quoted on stock exchanges in Britain, France and West
January 31, 1975

Germany in 1.7 years, all IBM stock in 143 days, all Exxon stock in 79 days, the Rockefeller family's wealth in six days-
We can be sure that the fortunes of Canada will be affected, as well. The point is this: we must be self-sufficient in energy. This must be our objective. Let me put forward the most serious point I have brought forward in my 15 years in the House of Commons. We have about 300 billion barrels of crude petroleum locked up in the tar sands, far more than the 60 billion barrels of crude oil in the Arab countries. If we can introduce tax policies which will encourage the activities of consortiums like Syncrude, we shall all be better off. Let us avoid confrontations between provinces.
The Minister of Finance can do nothing more important than encourage the development of our resources. I have criticized him in the past. Members on my side have not always agreed with my position. We in the Tory Party do not always think alike, because when everyone agrees it shows people are not thinking. Nevertheless, I have encouraged the minister to implement policies which will lead to the production of more oil. Questions have been raised concerning the production of petroleum-type fuels from natural gas. Let us remember that it costs $9 to produce one barrel of oil from the tar sands. I think it makes sense to try to find oil from conventional sources, as such oil can be produced at $3 or $4 per barrel. Remember that at one time it cost $600,000 to drill an oil well; now it may cost up to $2 million. What I am driving at is simply this, that security of energy supply from western Canada is important to Canada's economic stability. The Syncrude project, an important project for the extraction of some of our potential 300 billion barrels of oil, is threatened. Tax policy which is stopping development must be abandoned.
Having referred to the article in Time magazine, let me now review some of the history of the oil industry. We have come a long way since 1946. In that year, crude petroleum production in western Canada had declined to a measly 18,000 barrels a day and nearly 95 per cent of Canada's oil needs were imported. Today, on the other hand, we are self-sufficient. We use about one million barrels of crude petroleum per day. In eastern Canada we export a similar amount. We need two million barrels of oil per day. Pursuant to the national oil policy which was devised in previous years, the needs of eastern Canada were met by imports from Venezuela and Arab countries-that being the cheaper way to provide eastern Canada with oil-and the needs of western Canada were met by western crude. We export one million barrels to the U.S.A. and we import one million; hence we are self-sufficient.
Let me review the history of the oil industry. In 1946, drilling had come to a halt. Imperial Oil had drilled 133 dry holes, each costing approximately $600,000. The directors of the company met in Calgary, to call a halt to the spending of money. They had almost decided to build a plant which would produce synthetic gasoline from natural gas. The geologists attending the meeting convinced the directors to drill another well, even though 133 had already been drilled. The directors agreed and south-west of Edmonton, at Leduc, a successful well was drilled which at once caught fire. Americans were brought in to put the fire out. But that fire lit was an economic fire for
Income Tax
Canada. More important, that directors' meeting in Calgary, historically almost as important as the meeting leading to confederation, led to Canada becoming self-sufficient in energy.
We play around with the subject of energy as if it is not important. We must avoid confrontation between Alberta and the federal government or between the provinces. After all, the energy we produce in the west is important to Ontario and equally important for the maritimes and Quebec. It is important to us because it means we can be self-sufficient in energy. The United States, under President Ford's proposals, may implement gasoline rationing. We do not hear that kind of talk in this country. The meeting in 1946 in Calgary historically was just as important as Columbus's discovery of America. He saw a light and said he would sail on-" A light. Sail on, sail on"-He gave the world the grandest lesson, that is, do not quit just before success.
I ask the government to take another hard look at its policies. Let it, as the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain suggested so eloquently last evening, come to an agreement with the provinces in order to encourage exploration, to prevent the leaving of oil rigs as described by the Financial Post-drilling rigs that are leaving Canada for elsewhere.
At present, production in Saskatchewan is threatened because of the royalty policies of the Saskatchewan government and the federal government's tax on royalties. The extra cost of producing oil which has already been found is undermining the viability of the industry in Saskatchewan and this, in itself, would be enough to defeat any government if an election were called right now. Therefore, the national development of our energy resources is of top priority for Canada's continued economic health.
We talk about increasing benefits for pensioners, those on fixed incomes and those on social welfare. Why can't the people realize that much of our wealth can only come from the development of our natural resources? Our industry depends on energy. The government should consider, again, its taxing policies and leave the average wage earner of this country more take-home pay. After all, what counts is not the gross wage but what is left after taxes. My daughter is a secretary in a law firm in Edmonton and works-Liberal members may be interested to hear this-for the only Liberal candidate in Alberta who did not lose his deposit in the last federal election. She did not work for him at that time. She cannot take credit for that. The answer is this: I have looked at her pay cheque, and when you see the federal deductions one must appreciate it is impossible for her, with a husband going through law school, to live on the net pay. The same applies to the girls who work for my firm, as well as for firms all across the nation.
Let's get with it. It is possible, if we follow proper economic and financial policies. We were ridiculed during the election for our stand in favour of wage and price controls. I was told that in St. Catharines, when the Liberals spoke in criticism of Conservative policy, they talked about wage controls to the wage earners and price con-

January 31, 1975
Income Tax
trols to the farmers. As a result, three or four of my good friends, including men like Trevor Morgan and Ken Higson, were defeated. They were beaten by that kind of propaganda.
I beg the government to take a sane look at the tax policies of the nation as they affect individuals and corporations. I notice we do not hear anything today about corporate bums from hon. members to my left. The words of Mr. Lewis are forgotten. Today, he is like a lawyer with a closed-out file. And why? Because the unions in Oshawa are saying, "Give the corporations a tax cut or else their employees will be out of work." Broadbent has bent the policy because he realizes the economic reality behind the politics. Oh yes, it was a beautiful song at the time, because it was useful to be able to blame the corporations to win votes. For my part, Mr. Speaker, I am thankful for the kind of system we have. Behind the scenes I talk to members of all parties, especially when we get away from the House of Commons and go to a conference. I find we all think alike. We all have Canada at heart. Let us not, out of pure cussedness and politics, break the economics of this country.
May I call it one o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

Thank you, Madam Speaker. It is a privilege for me to take part in the debates when you are in the Chair.

In rising to take part in this debate, I wish to indicate first of all that I very strongly endorse some words which were used by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) in his budget statement. With your permission, Madam Speaker, I should like to quote these words because I think they are very important and have given the keynote to the approach that my party takes to the bill before us. In his budget speech, as reported at page 1422 of Hansard, the Minister of Finance said:
-the fiscal stimulus should come primarily from a further cut in taxes rather than from an additional increase in expenditure. I believe that tax cuts can help to reduce prices and costs directly or indirectly, and thus slow down the upward momentum of inflation. An indiscriminate or excessive increase in expenditures would exacerbate the pace of inflation.
That is what he says, but methinks our Minister of Finance speaks with forked tongue.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: And the parliamentary secretary.

The parliamentary secretary is not even speaking. The minister talks about
(Mr. Woolliams.]
reduction in expenditure. Last evening, in preparation for this debate, I made some simple calculations extending from 1968 to today in relation to the expenditures of this government, adjusted in accordance with one of the measures of inflation, the consumer price index. I found that in 1968 government expenditures amounted to $10.7 billion. If they were adjusted by the then operative consumer price index, they would have amounted the following year to $11,085 billion, or more or less $11.1 billion. The following year they would rise to $11.4 billion; then $11.8 billion, $12.8 billion, $13.8 billion. Finally, this year we could have expected, on the basis of the straight inflationary features to which we have unfortunately had to accustom ourselves, expenditures amounting to $14.9 billion-almost $15 billion.
But what do we actually find, Madam Speaker, over this particular period from 1968 to today? I know it cannot all be laid at the door of the present Minister of Finance, but certainly the latter figures show very clearly that a large portion can. I would say that by 1971 he had reached this magical $14.9 billion. By then this Minister of Finance was on the treasury bench as Minister of Finance and things started to take off. Instead of the $14.9 billion or $15 billion expenditure, we see today figures showing $26.3 billion. So the minister says on the one hand that we need to cut expenditures because this is going to depress inflation, yet this is the course he has been following through his three years in office. If this is not inflationary budgeting-almost doubling since 1972, from $14.8 billion to $26.3 billion, during his term of office-I have yet to see what is. And the minister makes comments like this!
It is evident that the government must pull in its belt, that it must cut expenditure. In this current budget he proposes to agree to reduce the tax levy by 3 per cent. My colleague from York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) has already commented on this aspect and said that the figure must be much higher. I, too, feel that the tax cut must be much more than that. However, I do not like to criticize without coming forward with positive, workable, practical alternatives and in my remarks this afternoon I am going to zero in on one particular sector of the economy in our society, namely, personal income tax and a special sector of our society subject to this form of income tax. In addition, I have another objective in view besides just cutting down government expenditure. I should like to see restored in this country the saving ethic which has been withered away. Others of my colleagues, and the parliamentary secretary as well, will be dealing with other aspects but I am going to confine myself to this particular sector of our community.
I have no patience with what I think can be described as the "leaning society"-those who lean on other people. I refer to a society whose citizens are encouraged to lean on governments for all their wants and requirements. This was not the way I was brought up and it is not the way I want to go on living. At the same time, I hasten to add that I strongly approve and firmly and heartily support every social service-and they must be available-for the needy in the community. The needy will long be with us and we must make provision for them. I do not criticize that aspect at all. But to make the whole of society lean on government for its requirements is, to my way of thinking, deplorable. We should never overlook the needy. But
January 31, 1975

in providing for them we must not lose sight of that other class of citizen, if you like the fortunate, the provident, those who have laid aside support for their later years so that they can enjoy them.
What is happening now to that class of society? What they have put aside has no value any more. It is being taxed out of existence and what is left to them is being withered away by inflation, fuelled-if I may use a term which has become rather common in these days of energy problems-by excessive government expenditure. I therefore feel that we must commend and encourage saving for one's future. But no encouragement is being given to savers today. Why is this so? Is it the desire of the government to make everyone dependent? Thankfully, there are still in our society those who are unwilling to become dependent and who still want to enjoy the independence for which they have striven. In one way or another we must encourage savings and see that there is value in those savings when the time comes to use them.
My proposal this afternoon is that taxes for all over 65 years of age be waived; that is, income taxes, capital gains taxes, taxes on superannuation, annuities, bonds, revenues from stocks and other investments, taxes on all revenue from all sources, and sales tax as well, should be waived for any person over 65 years of age. What I am anxious to do is put back in the hands of those over 65 years of age the funds that they have put aside and have been looking forward to using when they are no longer able to fit into the industrial life of our country. This would restore purchasing power in the hands of those who have struggled to lay aside savings in those days when savings earned more than Brownie marks. Saving was a virtue that was instilled in us in those days, a virtue which today is eroded and often even scorned. This is done by the manner in which the government more and more forces dependency on us.
This is one way to restore that virtue which, to my way of thinking, has much more value than this government is prepared to accord it. In short, what I seek to do with my proposal is increase the disposable income for the elderly, those who are no longer able to work full days in industry and who are living on fixed incomes, sometimes meagre fixed incomes but always dwindling fixed incomes, thanks to this government. I received a letter the other day from a pensioner in my riding about extra costs. I found it very moving. I suppose I should have thought of this before, but he put it in writing for me. He mentioned the repairs he needs to keep his house in order; to keep the rain and the wind from coming in. He referred to the difficulties he is having in paying for these repairs at current wage levels, and the difficulty he is having in using his savings to pay for these extra costs. He can no longer do the repairs himself. He once did them, as we all have done in our time. This government is depriving people of that sort of means to pay these extra costs, both by reducing their incomes and by allowing inflation to outstrip their capacity to pay.
I am sure the minister or his parliamentary secretary is going to say that the load has been reduced by extending the income tax deductions to all taxpayers and by permitting the first $1,000 of interest to be free of tax. At the

1974 bank short-term loan rates, this would be the equivalent of the interest on about $10,000. I suggest there are many people brought up in the work ethic who have worked for 35, 40 years and even more, who have been able to lay aside a bit more than that. They may in one way or another have an independent income exceeding that $1,000, but anything in excess is going to be taxed.
Furthermore-and I would like to point this out very clearly-there are a number of gimmicks in respect of this particular allowance which perhaps the Canadian people have not yet appreciated. They will become aware of this when the time comes to fill out their income tax forms three months from now. They will find that the total entitlement to that $1,000, if it is their due, is to be reduced by a number of interest charges. For example, if they already claim they are paying interest on their mortgages, the amount they are paying as interest will have to be deducted from this $1,000. This is a gimmick, a nice easy way of fooling the public, but the public has to be warned before it is too late.
Also, the minister or his parliamentary secretary, if he is talking to the minister these days-they may have to talk to that select group in the Prime Minister's office for this purpose-ought to get together with the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) to persuade him to lift the ceiling on earnings of pensioners so that pensioners may, through part-time work, supplement their incomes without penalty or fear of losing their guaranteed income supplement. This would serve a variety of worth-while purposes. It would restore to the pensioner his feeling of usefulness in society. Too often our pensioners feel they have been cast aside and can no longer fill a role in society. They can, and they should be encouraged to do so. They want to do so; but if they do, what happens? They get into an income bracket and either lose their guaranteed supplement or, worse, the Minister of Finance gets on their tails and requires them to pay income tax.
We should exempt these pensioners from taxes. This would enable pensioners to supplement their incomes without penalty and would help them to meet their daily needs. Because of the type of work to which pensioners might be limited, this would free others to work more productively at full-time jobs. I just pick this out of the hat as one example: pensioners might very well look after child-care centres, so that those who are now working in these centres could earn more wages for themselves and their families. This could be a part-time job for pensioners. This is what we must search to do for them.
There is another area I commend to the parliamentary secretary and, through him, to the minister, and that is the example of consumer price indexing which I used in my calculations last night. The minister has already borrowed a number of good features from this side of the House which he has put into the Income Tax Act. He borrowed the idea of indexing income taxes. This is fine, and I hope the minister is not immune from borrowing or accepting other good ideas when he hears them. Let me give him another good suggestion. The consumer price index is being used at the present time to index pensions so they will increase in accordance with inflationary pressures, and it is used in a variety of other ways. Let us look

at its effect on pensions. Is the minister aware that the current consumer price index, as revised in 1969, is designed to deal with specific classes of persons as set forward in a study prepared by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics, which I feel I still have to call it?
It is designed to meet the following three criteria: first of all, those living in Canadian urban centres with metropolitan populations exceeding 30,000; second, families ranging in size from two to six persons, consisting of any combination of adults or of adults and children-think of this in terms of pensioners-and third, those with annual incomes in 1967 ranging from $4,000 to $12,000. That is a fair spread, but there is an acknowledgement that it leaves out about 12 per cent at one end and about 14 per cent at the other end of the community. It is the 12 per cent at the lower end that I am concerned about today. These criteria fit only vaguely the class of persons I am concerned about today-sometimes two pensioners, sometimes only one; very seldom is it a matter of children. It is rarely a family of six to which these criteria are geared.
The other feature of the CPI which I find inapplicable to pensioners and those on limited and fixed incomes, and which I want to draw to the attention of the minister, is the weighing of the commodities in the index. I went to the trouble of finding out how the index was made up, and I got the shock of my life. Thinking of it from the perspective of the pensioner, I find it shocking. We find here 25 per cent allowed on food, 31.4 per cent on housing, 11 per cent on clothing and 15 per cent on transportation of which 3 per cent is for gasoline. I am thinking of the pensioners in my riding who have not been near a gas pump for a long time, unfortunately.
The following is ridiculous, laughable: 4 per cent on health and personal care, 6.8 per cent on recreation, education and reading, and 5.9 per cent on tobacco and alcohol. That is how it is broken down. You have to be kidding! The facts of the situation for pensioners are quite different from that particular breakdown. I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is walking out. I hope he is not doing so because he thinks I am accusing him of spending 6 per cent on tobacco and alcohol. In fact, he is probably saving that amount on tobacco and alcohol.
A little more, now.
Others must be pretty high to make up for my zero.

There is another element in this particular breakdown. One-third is supposed to go on housing. If they are renting then they may possibly be paying a third of their income, perhaps even more; but if that section applies to house owners-and many pensioners are house owners-I suspect that the proportion would be entirely different. Their houses are probably paid off and they only have municipal taxes to deal with. Almost the same amount is allowed for recreation, education and reading as for tobacco and alcohol. In the breakdown we find that 15 per cent is allowed for transportation and 4.5 per cent for health and personal care. The whole formula is wrong for pensioners.
(Mr. Munro (Esquimalt-Saanich).]
Let us look at it even more closely within some of the items of the breakdown. Under the item for food, for example, 21 per cent is presumed to be spent at home and 4 per cent away from home, eating in restaurants. That I cannot accept. That is not possible on a pensioner's income. In the breakdown, 7 per cent is spent on meat, 3 per cent on dairy products and 3 per cent on fruit. That does not add up, either. The high cost of meat may account for that, but we are not talking about that. It is presumed that 7 per cent of the disposable income is spent on meat. If they are eating meat at all, I suspect that they are spending a good deal more on it; but I fear, having been in some of the supermarkets in my riding and having watched some of the pensioners in my constituency shopping for their groceries, that they are not spending 7 per cent of their income on meat. They are looking at meat, thinking it would be very nice to take it home, and then putting it down and going to another counter.
Then, how much baby food do pensioners buy? Do they spend the same amount on it as they spend on sugar? That is what the consumer price index suggests. Here is another funny item. Do women on pension spend almost 4 per cent of their income on clothes and allow the men less than 3 per cent on clothes?
That is probably true.

This is women's year. I think we should go back to equality at least. Do they need to spend anything at all on children's wear, although there is a provision here for 1.5 per cent of income on children's wear? Footwear for children is not to be included in that 1.5 per cent because it appears under a different heading. There is another breakdown for recreation on which 1.3 per cent is allowed, which includes bicycles, cameras and toys. Perhaps toys may be for grandchildren but I suspect they are not buying many toys for themselves, and very few bicycles.
One can study this index in considerably more detail. I have more particulars here that I would be very happy to bring to the attention of the government, but I think I have indicated enough so far to suggest that if we are to go on using the current consumer price index, we must weight it in favour of the lower and fixed income sectors of our population. I would prefer a pensioners' index which would adjust pension incomes in accordance with pensioners' needs in inflationary times. That, I think, is the ultimate objective-a pensioners' index.
I am not a statistician and therefore cannot reshuffle the weightings to create a pensioners' index at this moment, nor would it be possible in the time during this debate to work one out. I do submit, however, that the task must be done eventually. I suggest, meanwhile, that we should have soon, but preferably now, a weighted CPI favouring the lower income sectors of our society and discriminating against the higher income sectors, so that instead of being applied as a straight 10.8-if that is the annual increase in CPI-that it be, say, 14 per cent for the lower income people and down to 7 per cent for those on higher income.
I suggest that such a weighting of the CPI be used for all purposes, for indexing pensions, income tax levies,

superannuation benefits, pay increases in the public service both civil and military and, finally, that in the long run we work toward the compilation of a new and distinct pensioners' index tailored especially to the needs and the consuming pattern of pensioners. These are some of the positive ways which we might use to relieve the lot of the disadvantaged without burdening the treasury. So I am back where I started. Indeed, probably on balance we would be reducing the charges on the treasury by a considerable amount, thereby reducing government expenditures.
In summary, my plea is for a substantial cut in government expenditures, restoration of the saving ethic and elimination of the cult of dependency that is being nurtured in our society by this government, waiver of all federal taxes for pensioners, taxes on all forms of income, capital gains tax and sales tax, and an adjustment of the CPI or the development of a pensioners' index. Finally, in order to increase disposable income to pensioners, we should lift the ceiling on earnings of pensioners to allow them to supplement their income without fear of losing that little increment which they receive, the guaranteed income supplement.

Madam Speaker, the purpose of the bill before us is to effect changes in the personal and corporate income tax proposals in the November 18 budget. Before commenting on these changes I would like to say a few words about the assumptions which underlie that budget. You do not have to be an economist or a highly educated person to understand that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) proposes a budget, he has to operate under basic assumptions which really amount to forecasts by members of his department concerning, for example, growth possibilities, employment and unemployment in Canada.
One of the most important assumptions underlying the finance minister's budget of November 18 was that Canada would have a real growth rate of 4 per cent for 1975 and this would produce, in his words, approximately half a million new jobs. His budget made no forecast about the expected unemployment rate, but his deficit forecast for this year strongly suggests that we are going to have an unemployment rate considerably higher than the approximate 5.4 per cent which was being experienced when the minister and his staff presented the budget.
I think it is safe to say that we will have in the vicinity of 7 per cent unemployment in this country, which will bring us back to the days of 1960 and 1961 as an average unemployment figure adjusted for changes. Despite all his recent ballyhoo about the budget, that it has been designed to fight inflation and increase growth, the minister and those advising him are still old-time religionists regarding fiscal and monetary matters.
In fact, inflation is going to be fought by the minister by creating unemployment, but not so obviously as the government did during 1970 and 1971. They have at least learned that lesson; that was obvious in the budget. Nevertheless, the government is using monetary and fiscal tools up to a certain level, and it is going to talk
Income Tax
about restraints in various sectors of the economy in order to control inflation. But in reality the policies and the lack of policies create increasing unemployment and you fight inflation by increasing unemployment and hope that prices will come down in this way. It is a beautiful game where you have your neighbour, the giant, who is able to play and has been able to play the same game until very recently. Of course, the stimulative measures taken in the United States recently will take at least six months to affect that economy.
I fundamentally disagree with the assumptions underlying the minister's budget. Many countries have organized in the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development, known as OECD. The research people for this organization make forecasts for many countries in the world, including Canada. The Minister of Finance, in making his assumptions, has forecast our expected growth rate at 4 per cent. The OECD's most recent study suggests that instead of having a 4 per cent real growth rate in terms of output in Canada for this year, the best we could hope for would be a 1 per cent or possibly a 2 per cent growth rate. This would mean practically no new jobs created in Canada, and much higher levels of unemployment.
All of us can expect to hear in the next year from the Minister of Finance and from the cabinet that this increase in unemployment will be the result of an increase in the labour force rather than because of deficiencies in their own policies, unless they are corrected very soon by a mini-budget that will recognize that in the short run we can no longer fight the evil of inflation by creating more unemployment, and that fiscal and monetary tools must be used by the minister in the short run to correct the increasing level of unemployment which can rise to 7 per cent very quickly. While he and others are pushing up the level of full employment to 5 per cent, the fact is that they will create the 7 per cent unemployment that I am talking about, and that will create an immense hardship for people and distort the economy more than we have seen in recent years.
There is more disturbing evidence emanating from recent figures released by Statistics Canada which, while it makes for dry reading, is very suggestive in terms of what we can expect in regard to employment and unemployment in the Canadian economy this year. I would go so far as to say that those figures suggest that we are already well into a recession. The Minister of Finance has difficulty with that word, and that is understandable in human terms. He prefers to talk about inflation, on the one hand, and lack of adequate growth on the other, instead of calling a spade a spade and telling the Canadian people that we are now in a period of stagflation, or slumpflation in which we have, for the first time in peacetime Canadian history, double-digit price increases which are very strongly embedded in the economy at a time when we are approaching 7 per cent unemployment in this country on a seasonally adjusted basis. If that is not recession, what can it possibly be? How much unemployment must we have before the government will admit that, instead of talking about a period of inflation and slow growth?

As far as the recent figures are concerned, there has been a decline or a stagnation in the growth figures which have been released. Most economists see the trend I have been describing as evidence of poor economic performance. That is not peculiar to this country, of course, but sometimes members on the other side, especially the Minister of Finance, are inclined to stick out their chests too far because of our success in comparison with other countries.
We know very well that the things we are rich in- wheat, oil, pulp and paper-have demanded a tremendous price on international markets in the last few years and this has given us an advantage. Thank God we have had it. But it is not through the policies of the government. I suggest that if they stick their chests out too far on this issue, they might find themselves eating humble pie in the next few months when the export figures become avail: able and we run into serious trouble because of the decline in housing starts and the state of the economies of the United States and other countries. I mentioned that the minister had failed to forecast the unemployment rate for 1975-76 in the budget. I have already mentioned that independent researchers are predicting a norm of 7 per cent. I should like to look at some of the individual items, Madam Speaker, as they refer to the bill before us. Many of them show that the legislation is geared to the rich and the large corporations rather than people in the low and middle-income categories. If that sounds like an NDP line, let me try to buttress it with some evidence.
Let us ask ourselves about these tax cuts and what there is in the budget for the ordinary taxpayer. There is the tax cut which was in the budget of last May. I think the minister was trying to fool the House when he suggested there was a minimum cut of $150 in taxes. All he did was add the $100 that was in the mini-budget of February, 1973, to the $50 proposed, making it look like a tax cut of $150 instead of the $50 it actually is. We know that a tax cut of $50 works out to about 97 cents a week. That is some tax cut when you consider there is nothing in this budget to control the cost of living! The hon. member for Windsor West (Mr. Gray) put my thinking in cogent form yesterday when in the course of debate he said:
This bill and the budget seem to be saying that inflation hits the higher income person harder than the one earning a low income. But surely it is just the opposite. Lower income people spend a greater proportion of their income on food than those earning more. Therefore, why should a man earning $6,000 be given only $214 more, while the man earning $30,000 will be given $622 more through tax reductions? This is done in both cases to meet "part of the increase in the cost of food". This is the purpose of the tax cut, according to the budget speech.
The bill proposes that no one would get a tax reduction of less than $200 or more than $750; that is, the cut would have a floor of $200 and a ceiling of $750.
We could quarrel with that, but that is his interpretation.
One could ask, therefore, why the proposal did not call for a higher floor and a lower ceiling. In other words, why was there not a higher minimum tax reduction and a lower maximum tax reduction to ensure that the lower and middle-income Canadian would get even more disposable income through tax reductions
(Mr. Hogan.]
and the imbalance toward the higher income earner would be less than it would otherwise be?
As I mentioned, Madam Speaker, that puts my thinking on the tax cuts in very cogent form. We should be pledged to help the low income earner in this country, considering the gross inequities that still exist in the distribution of income. Now let me say a word about the pensioners. The government even failed in this budget to mention an increase in the basic old age pension. It is true that they made an exemption for the first $1,000 for extra pension moneys other than pensions which are universal in this country. We in the NDP always welcome any improvement made in the position of senior citizens. Accordingly, we welcome even this anaemic improvement for senior citizens announced in the budget, some of which applies to the year 1974 and some to 1975.
However, this is an important point: all of these benefits apply only to 40 per cent of persons over 65 who have income other than their old age pension and general income supplement. These 40 per cent get their benefits through tax relief, (a) by means of $1,000 interest income exemption starting in 1974; (b) the $1,000 private income exemption in 1975; and (c) the right of one spouse to claim the special exemption for both spouses. But the fact is, Madam Speaker, that between 50 per cent and 60 per cent of Canadians over 65 rely completely on the old age pension and the general income supplement. What they need-and this applies to more than a million old age pensioners in this country-is a substantial increase in the basic amount of old age security, which should be at the very least $200 per month per person. Year after year, as hon. members know, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) of the NDP has a motion on the order paper concerning this matter. His motion really ought to be accepted.
We think that a $200 payment for each woman and man over 65 years of age should be made available in the next few years, so that brought down one year at a time it would reach age 60 within a decent length of time. We have still a long way to go toward correcting the inequities that exist when we have 60 per cent of our old age pensioners living on the old age pension and the supplement. The budget and the bill before us do nothing to correct the situation.
What about housing, Madam Speaker? We have had a debate on housing. I will not repeat a lot of the arguments that have been advanced, but let us talk about the registered home ownership savings plan. The provisions of a registered home ownership savings plan in this budget is a carry-over from last May's budget. This means that people who can afford to put money aside will put $1,000 annually into a savings plan for the purchase of a home, or furniture with which to furnish that home. This program will probably be effective for many in Canada. But how many low-income people will benefit? How many members can go back to their ridings and count great numbers of people who can set aside $1,000 annually? I know my riding is relatively poor, and I also know that this program will help only a very small percentage of my constituents.

January 31, 1975
It is obvious, as any statistician will tell you, that only the wealthier people in our society will be able to take advantage of this program, not those on middle or low-incomes whose housing needs are scarcely being met by this budget. I am surprised at the suggestion of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson), that the government's housing program will meet the needs of our people. The pot-pourri the minister is offering will do little to satisfy the housing needs of the middle and low-income people of this country. Surely he learned his lesson yesterday when talking with provincial ministers. I know that many Canadians live in centres like Toronto and Montreal, but many others who ought to be considered live in smaller centres, such as those in the Atlantic region.
It is true that we should encourage more private ownership of homes, but we must also encourage greater expenditure on public housing, condominium housing, co-operative housing and the like. The budget does little in this area. We must recognize that although market forces have a role to play, the social needs of the Canadian people must be met. Therefore, the government and the decisionmakers in the cabinet must act for the good of the many in need. If that means that there is to be a redistribution of income, so be it. When will this country have the guts to do something like that? How many more Croll reports do we need to convince the powers that be that we need more equitable distribution of incomes in this country, either through the income tax process or through special services like housing? In my opinion this budget does little to help low-income people meet their present housing needs.
A new provision in the budget allows people to deduct from income funds to be used in the building of apartments. For medium-sized and large cities this provision makes sense, but what is the advantage of it to smaller communities?
Very little.

In my riding, where the average income is $6,800, this provision is not worth a damn. We need more money from Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation directed to the Nova Scotia housing commission and other provincial housing commissions for putting up cooperative housing, condominiums, public housing and the like. I suggest, again, that the ordinary citizen will not benefit from this measure. It will help those in higher income brackets. Admittedly, they need help, too; but our first concern should be for those in the lower income bracket. Surely that is obvious.
Let me say a word about distribution of incomes and wealth in this country, because the income tax changes proposed under this bill fail to encourage real redistribution of incomes. Remember, behind these dry figures are human beings who are suffering in this country which enjoys, according to the figures one uses, the second or third highest standard of living in the world. I shall refer to the incomes of families in the period 1965-72. According to Statistics Canada, in 1965 the bottom 60 per cent of Canadians earned 34.2 per cent of the income of this country; the top 20 per cent earned 41.4 per cent. In 1972, according to the latest official figures available, the
Income Tax
bottom 60 per cent saw a drop in their income; they earned only 32.2 per cent of the national net income, while the top 20 per cent earned 42.9 per cent. Again, these are not my figures; they are the figures of Statistics Canada. They show that during the so-called years of the just society under the Liberal government, the income gap between rich and poor widened.
The disparities in wealth are even more startling. According to the most recent figures I have seen in 1970, the top 50 per cent of families or individuals in this country owned 93 per cent of our wealth, the top 10 per cent of families or individuals owned 41.8 per cent, and the top 1 per cent owned 12 per cent. Clearly, we have a long way to go before wealth in this country is distributed equitably. There is no reason for us to stick out our chests about what we have done in the post-war period. Do the figures I have mentioned show that in this country there is greater equity than before? No. Are we moving toward more equitable distribution of income? No.
I mentioned, in passing, the Croll report. When will the cabinet heed the message? According to the Croll report, between 1945 and 1971, or 1972, despite welfare measures introduced by the Liberals, which were first suggested by our party, the gap between poor and rich in this country remained as wide as ever. The poor, in terms of their share of income and wealth, are still relatively as far behind the rich as they were in 1945. Why? The main reason is that the tax system is stacked against the poor. As Senator Croll pointed out, even if our poor people are given a break under our progressive income tax system, they are hit with property taxes, excise taxes of all kinds and sales taxes. In total, these taxes are so regressive that the income growth of our poorer people has not kept pace with the income growth of the people at the top of the income scale.
Surely this cannot go on forever, even though our poorer people may be regarded as invisible and do not have much political power. Surely a government which says we should share our wealth with the rest of the world will agree that we should share wealth with the rest in this country more equitably. The time for action is now. Under our political system, the best time to do something is when you need not immediately consider political consequences. If that sounds like political cynicism, we must be realistic. The government may be reluctant to make changes in the tax structure immediately before an election. But when it has a majority and an election is not imminent, surely it should be able to move towards revolutionizing, if you like, the tax structure of this country for the sake of our low-income groups.
Coming from the Atlantic region I want to make this point. I want to say, along with the other criticisms I have made, and which I think are justified, about the budget and the proposals facing us in this bill, that there is nothing in that budget, as there was nothing in the May budget, about regional disparities in this country. And that is the basis of our difficulties in trying to stay loyal to the Canada which we love. We all realise that the regional problems facing this country are very severe, but when in the political situation you have underlying economic disparity continuing as it has done for so long in the Atlantic

region, and when we have a chance to correct it through budgetary measures, then, I think, Madam Speaker, that we should take advantage of that opportunity.
When I look at the figures concerning the Department of Regional Economic Expansion-and I am a member of the standing committee dealing with that department- and when I see the increase in the expenditure for this year, there is little or no improvement when the factor of inflation is taken into consideration.

Hear, hear!
