Now I would like to turn to some comments I have to make relative to the discussions which have taken place in this House during this week. Yesterday, in reply to a question from the member for Vancouver South (Mr. Fraser), the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro), in trying to defend his colleague the Minister of Finance, said that the Minister of Finance, when giving his famous speech last Monday in which he defended his position in trying to bring about voluntary wage and price restraints, didn't put the load on any one sector when he talked about the changing nature of inflation. And, as you recall, I got up in the House and quoted from what the Minister of Finance said.
He said in that speech that you had a change in the type of inflation, which by the way during the election campaign was an imported inflation, but now it seems it has changed so that you need to go to all of the different sectors in the economy. But he says it has changed from being what we call a demand-pull type of inflation, including the importation of inflation, to what we call a cost-push type of inflation. He doesn't use these words, but he says that the inflation which we have now, the major cause of it-and he used the word "major"-is due to the "rapid escalation of wages and salaries", and that inflation now is different from the inflation that was in the past.
The Minister of Labour tried to deny that the Minister of Finance said it was a major or a principal concern. Now it is true that in another talk that the Minister gave he mentioned that he was concerned about other sectors sharing the burden with labour on this thing, but he did say that wage and salary increases were the culprit, and I think there is nothing wrong with that as long as you've got the guts enough to back it up in the end.
If this is true and if the minister has the evidence to show in terms of statistics-and of course we can all battle about this-then he should confront Joe Morris, who is head of the Canadian Labour Congress; he should confront him with his statistics and say, "Look, the ball-
(Mr. Hogan.]
game has changed." But we have the Canadian Labour Congress the next day and Stan Little of CUPE coming out, and the third man, Bill Mahoney of the Steel Workers Union, saying they still have to catch up. They have said it isn't any kind of a wage-push inflation under the cost-push interpretation in which they were the culprits, but their members still have to catch up. We can understand that they are political animals like ourselves, but there must be some objective evidence that the minister has to show them, because there is a direct contradiction, one against the other, despite the attempt of the Minister of Labour to try to say that there is not.
We recognize that there is immense difficulty in bringing these groups together; there is an immense difficulty involved in trying to stabilize an economy which is fighting the problems of inflation as well as a condition of high unemployment.
We need honest answers and I cannot understand why, just after an election when you are facing a full four years in office, if you have firm convictions on such matters and they are based on firm evidence and criteria, if, for example, there is evidence of loss of productivity and therefore higher unit costs in the manufacturing sector, which is much more easy to measure than the service sector, ministers should come out and say it. Nobody is just going to go out and defend labour at this special time in our history if the evidence to the contrary is there. The ministers concerned owe it to the Canadian people, and they owe it to us all to do that type of thing.
I just want to suggest in closing that I don't want the Minister of Finance to listen to something which some of the Tory speakers during this debate are telling him to do, that is, be principally concerned about the rate and level of expenditures in this country. But even though they are personally convinced of this, the minister should avoid their advice when unemployment is likely to rise to 7 per cent or more. When you put the Atlantic region into the picture it could go from 10.7 per cent in December to probably 15 or 16 per cent. It is tough, and we have to fight that short-run unemployment problem. The Finance Minister has to come here in April or May and say, "Look, my budget cuts weren't deep enough; we've got to ease the money supply and we have to get together with the provinces and put on special public works." On the other hand, we have to avoid saying we have to restrain ourselves and then cover over with a veneer that refuses to call a spade a spade on income shares. He will have to come up with some hard evidence as we suggested he might.
It will be unpopular for me to say this, but I will say it anyway: the finance minister has two strikes against him now. The first is the psychological effect of the introduction of the notion that a 50 per cent increase was going to be taken at one point by us, and the fact that there seems now to be a feeling amongst the labour leaders in this country that he says one thing before them and another before the business community. That is the reason I think he has two strikes against him. But I and others will support him if he will just come out and give us the facts. Let us interpret the facts, and if wage increases generally outstrip the cost of living increases, let us see the statistics. If the productivity ratio is going down in the manu-
January 31, 1975

facturing sector let us see the figures, and this will form a basis on which we can judge.
I also refer to a response the minister made to someone's question this week that the people of Canada, by not putting the Conservatives in power in July, had voted against a wage and price freeze. I refuse to accept that non sequitur of the Minister of Finance. There can well be other reasons which we don't have to document now and make a great production about as to why they lost the election. One thing in relation to this matter is that during the election they did a darned poor job of explaining what they meant by a wage and price freeze, and they were even helped by the press during the middle of the campaign who started calling it an all-embracing incomes policy.
An all-embracing incomes policy is different from a wage and price freeze. An all-embracing incomes policy has been approved by George Meany and by many of the Democrats in the United States because it includes wages, interest income, rental income and dividends. Therefore it makes for equity and the burden doesn't go just on the wage-earner and the salary-earner. I think this has to be reconsidered, though probably not for the immediate future.
I suspect that the Minister of Finance is still really relying on what I call the old time religion. My evidence of that is that no one in this House can deny that increasing unemployment is being used to fight inflation in this country. We are heading for 7 per cent unemployment which will result in prices having to come down, even in an economy so much controlled by the large corporations of this country.
Mr. ]. Robert Howie (York-Sunbury): Madam Speaker, once again I should like to congratulate you, sitting in your accustomed place, and to say that you are certainly the most attractive Speaker this House has ever had.
Hear, hear!

I should like to make a few brief comments on matters relating to Bill C-49. I should like to begin by expressing, on behalf of the people of York-Sunbury, my best wishes to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), who has displayed the good judgment to visit New Brunswick and enjoy the outstanding natural advantages of St. Andrews-by-the-Sea. While I disagree with a number of the minister's ideas as to the best way to fight inflation, I realize that his heart is in the right place, and that he is performing the duties of his difficult portfolio to the best of his ability.
I would like to discuss three matters of immediate concern. The first item of concern is the government's intention to move into the field of resource taxation. The eleventh annual review of the Economic Council stated at page 113:
The problem of ensuring adequate and secure future supplies of energy in Canada is not a new one, nor did it begin with the events of late 1973, when Arab oil producers imposed a selective embargo and crude oil prices were increased at unprecedented rates. The actions of the major oil producing countries have, however, forced Canadians to re-examine their plans for development of
Income Tax
their energy resources, to revise policy, and to implement new measures at a pace in line with the ever-changing international situation.
Perhaps it was for this reason that the federal government decided to move into the field of resource taxation. As a member of parliament from the Atlantic provinces I am very much interested in seeing a strong central government that shares the good things our country has to offer with all Canadians, and acts to remedy regional disparity. I believe that the central government has been strong and had done much to distribute tax revenues and fight regional disparity, but I feel that in dealing with Alberta it has not always been just. The lack of consultation with the provinces before November 18, 1974, goes against the spirit of co-operative federalism. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has stated, referring to the west: "If they feel alienated, let them participate". I suggest that this would be an excellent opportunity for such participation.
The finance minister on January 28, as reported in Hansard at page 2694, quoted the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) as saying:
The federal government must retain a sufficient portion of the tax fields in Canada to enable it to discharge its direct constitutional responsibilities and to assist provinces with low tax potential so as to enable them to furnish a national standard of services to the Canadian citizens residing within their boundaries.
The minister said that he agreed with those words. I compliment the minister on his excellent and apparently improved reading habits. The question is not the words used but, rather, the meaning and their implementation. I suggest that if the Minister of Finance understood what the Leader of the Opposition said when he spoke those words, we would have no problem now. Today we do have a problem; we have strained relations between Ottawa and Alberta. We have a loss of confidence in our economic climate. We have the possibility of the Syncrude development failing. And Canada and the free world need the Syncrude development.
I feel that the government does not understand the west and the fears and anxieties of western Canadians. The west wants and needs to use its oil revenues, which may last only another four years, to develop an industrial base. For years industrial development has been encouraged and subsidized in Canada by tariff protection and taxation policies. All Canadians have paid more for manufactured goods to help develop our country. The west and the east have not directly shared in very much of this development. Yet when the opportunity arrives for the west to develop, the federal government seems to diminish it and, in so doing, argues that it is protecting easterners in respect to the price of oil, and will help the west develop as time goes on.
As it now stands this increased taxation and the way it was imposed would be very detrimental for not just the industry but the country as a whole. The eleventh annual report of the Economic council of Canada goes on to state at page 140 that:
The amount of rent (tax) collected, at a given resource selling price, will likely affect industry motivation; that is, increased rent will tend to discourage industry exploration and the development of new energy sources. To the extent that the rent collected by governments is used to promote further exploration, disincentives

January 31, 1975
Income Tax
to industry may be partially or wholly offset. However if these funds are not used this way, while some other sectors of the economy may benefit in the short run, the resultant reduction in the volume of proved energy resources will affect the entire economy in the longer run. Any short-term advantage to present consumption will be realized at the expense of future consumption in the form of higher prices. The amount of rent collected by governments must not be such as to discourage adequate development of higher cost energy sources, which will gradually replace conventional reserves, unless governments are prepared to either accept exceptionally steep price increases at a later date or to rely upon important supplies ...
Clearly the allocation of rents from existing resources is a complex one that must be considered with a view to both short and long run consequences. It cannot be settled by any one body, but it must take into account the interests of federal and provincial governments, industry, and consumers, both in the short run and over the long term.
By 1980 Canada will likely be a net importer of oil unless new reserves are found and developed. This will require planning and co-operation. If the government had given indications in the past not only that its word was good but that its performance was good, we would not be in the position we are today. However, all that is now behind us. What we need now is a show of good faith on the part of the federal government. It is better to light a small candle than to curse the darkness.
I suggest to the minister that he postpone taxation of oil royalties and give an unmistakable signal of good gaith by amending this section of the bill to provide for it to come into force on a date to be fixed by the governor general in council. He should indicate that he does not want to disallow the reduction of oil royalties, that he wants to use reason and not force, that he is the spokesman for a just government.
The second item I wish to discuss is old age pensions. As it now stands, a married couple receiving old age pensions is in a worse position, as far as paying income tax is concerned, than two single people living together receiving old age pensions. I ask the minister, rather than arrange a complicated formula to correct this inequity, to give our senior citizens a real break and remove money received from the old age pension and supplement from taxable income. Our senior citizens deserve at least this much so that financial problems will not be a real difficulty for them.
My final point, Mr. Speaker, refers to the registered home ownership savings plan. All I wish to say on this is that when the minister feels the need to fulfil an election promise, could he please ensure that the program is ready to be set up before it is announced? The Canadian taxpayers have a right to know how they can benefit from this program on their 1974 income tax returns, rather than be told that "Yes, the program applies to 1974, but you will have to wait until the end of February to find out how it works".
Finally, I should very much like to endorse the tax reduction program that has been, recommended by my colleague, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens). I feel such an imaginative and substantial reduction in income tax would be reflected by greater employment and more taxpayers, and that our revenues would not be seriously impaired. I believe this is a good incentive, and an idea the minister should very seriously consider.

Madam Speaker, I should like to speak briefly about a specific aspect of the Income Tax Act. I refer to the much publicized $1,000 clause which supposedly permits a person to reduce his or her taxable income by $1,000 providing that person has earned at least $1,000 in interest from Canadian investments. As outlined in Item 35 in the 1974 income tax guide, a taxpayer's eligible interest must also first be reduced by the total of all interest deductions claimed in the computation of income from other sources reported on the return. This all sounds pretty good at first reading, but closer examination reveals some apparent shortcomings, and even discriminations.
First, it would appear that if an individual owns an apartment building and has a mortgage or bank loan against the property on which he is paying interest charges, then the interest charges must be offset against the exemption under the $1,000 interest earned allowance. If this is actually the case then I feel there are a number of reasons why the situation should be rectified.
The purpose of other main points in the budget was to encourage investment in rental accommodation and property. The above-mentioned situation would do the opposite. Furthermore, the purpose of the $1,000 exemption was to produce investment income, the net of which is taxable. I feel, therefore, that bank or mortgage interest paid in connection with the operation of a business should be considered as having to be deductions from the $1,000 exemption allowance.
Another apparent discrimination in this section of the Income Tax Act is that, in order for a married couple to receive any benefit of exemption on the wife's earnings, it would appear that she would have had to earn over $1,806 during the taxable year and, therefore, not be a deduction herself. This is, of course, when the husband has earned the bulk of the couple's income.
This appears to be a strong discrimination against the spouse of a taxpayer, and would in most cases be a discrimination against women. Because of the fact that many times it is the spouse who acquires the savings of a married couple, this loophole would be a sizeable detriment to investments. I call it a loophole because I am giving the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) the benefit of the suggestion that this slip-up was inadvertent.
With the cost of living as high as it is, and rising at the unprecedented rate that it is, the low and middle income people of this country need all the tax relief available to help them make ends meet. This does not mean introducing a much ballyhooed tax exemption that is comprised of a bunch of promises and fine print. The intent of the legislation, meagre as it might be, has to be effectively met. To ensure this we must be certain that all Canadian taxpayers will be eligible to claim the full benefit of the $1,000 deduction. Therefore these discrepancies must be investigated and rectified.

Madam Speaker, in availing myself of the privilege of participating in this debate I do so not only because we have the opportunity of discussing the policy of the government, but also because we can give some thought to the role of parlia-
January 31, 1975

ment in relation to government expenditures. Just before I move into that aspect of my speech I should like to make a reference or two to statements made by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan). I am glad he is still here as I would not want to say this while he was out of the House.
I should just like to point out that no member of this party proposes any cut in expenditure that would adversely affect the wellbeing of the people of this country. That has never been proposed, and it is not our intention. I just want to make that correction because, although I realize that the implication was not deliberate, it could appear to be if left in the record without a statement of this kind. We believe there are plenty of areas in which the government can reduce expenditures without -adversely affecting the services provided the Canadian people.
Perhaps I should refer to the recent facts brought out in relation to CIDA. Here again I want to make it abundantly clear that I am in favour of aid to those nations that need it and can use it effectively, but I am opposed to the indiscriminate spending of taxpayers' money under circumstances that will not bring the desired results.
There was one other reference made by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond to which I should like to respond. He was attempting to conduct a post-mortem regarding the last election campaign. Perhaps it would be more profitable if he were to look at his own party and try to ascertain why it was that it was so drastically reduced numerically in this parliament as compared with the last parliament. Perhaps having made those two comments I can now proceed to what I had intended to say in this debate.
I referred to the fact earlier that this debate gives us the opportunity to discuss the role of parliament in relation to government expenditures. I am sure we all agree that the struggle for parliamentary supremacy in matters of finance historically parallels the struggle for democracy in our western society. These two struggles are closely linked.
It is consistently true that in a nation where the people or their representatives do not control, or at least oversee the expenditure of public moneys, democracy suffers and democratic institutions die. In those circumstances the democratic process is replaced by some form of totalitarianism. If this consolidation of power over the purse in the hands of the few is coupled with incompetence, dishonesty and deliberate manipulation of information, then democracy cannot last very long.
In Canada I am afraid that over the last six and a half years, since this administration took the reins of government, the people's control over the purse, and their representatives' check on public expenditures both have slipped very badly, resulting in a definite downgrading of the democratic process. It used to be that ministers of the Crown had to stand in their places in this House and defend any expenditure contained in their estimates. I can look back possibly on more years than I sometimes care to remember.
Over 20 years ago, when I first came into this House, I can remember how the estimates were brought before the
Income Tax
committee of the whole. When the estimates of a particular department were called the officials were seated immediately in front of the minister and the minister could be grilled in depth by the opposition, or in some cases by supporters of the government, on the reasons for the expenditures and the advisability of various projects included in the estimates.
But I was amazed and shocked when I came back, after a brief respite, in 1972 to find out that this control had been eroded, and that the rules implemented by the administration from 1968 to 1972 did away with all that, and authorized the expenditures of literally billions of dollars under the new House rules, in sometimes just a matter of a very few hours. I said I was shocked to see the erosion that had taken place, and as we compare the two systems I feel that we, the representatives of the people, have to quite an extent lost control over the purse strings or even the opportunity of discussing government expenditures in the House of Commons.
Since 1968, when the present crowd gained control of the purse, they have been spending like drunken sailors, and let me apologize to the sailors, of course. Federal spending has increased 140 per cent in only six and half years.
In 1968 the federal government cost each man, woman, and child in Canada $590 a year. Today it costs each one $1,300 a year. This increase has been from $12 billion in federal expenditures in 1968 to $30 billion in 1974. That increase is bad enough, but what is worse is that this staggering increase has not included one major new social or economic program. I know that other programs have been improved, but no new major social or economic programs have been brought forward.
Between the years 1973-1974 and 1974-1975 the total government expenditures on a national accounts basis, as recorded at page 1431 of Hansard, increased from some $23 billion to $30 billion, or some 30 per cent, again not because of any new social or economic program but primarily because of the waste, duplication and inefficiency of the government.
The most noteworthy example of this spending spree is the one that hit the headlines over the last few weeks. I am, of course, speaking about CIDA. This is one area where it has been documented that the government is spending the public's money like the drunken sailor I mentioned earlier. The agency found the fiscal year coming to a close and had to scramble head over heels, literally, to try to spend the last $117 million of its allocation for the fiscal year. This fact was not denied by its president, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, at a recent news conference in Halifax, and I quote from the Ottawa Journal's front page of January 29, 1975:
"While charges of inefficiency against CIDA are totally incorrect", he said he accepted criticism that the agency "scrambled to spend a $117 million surplus of budget before the end of the fiscal year".
The president of the agency does not even try to deny what the government has been denying ever since this story hit the papers, thanks to the investigative reporting of Bob McKeown and Chris Cobb of the Journal staff.

CIDA has been called a sick joke, a state within a state, an empire presided over by a dictatorial president with an imperial style. To quote the Ottawa Journal of January 11, 1975:
Critics of Gerin-Lajoie start with his imperial style. His vanity is an Ottawa in-joke, from the personal staff of six aides-larger than that of any cabinet minister-to the one-third of his time spent travelling abroad to be introduced as "Le President", a title easily misunderstood.
I could go on and on about this agency. There certainly have been enough charges made against it and its president to warrant a special investigation of its and his activities.
It is really incredible to me why the government does not permit a parliamentary inquiry. It would seem to me that if these facts are not as related, if the facts are not as stated in the newspaper reports, if the allegations are incorrect, the government would be glad to have an inquiry and to clarify the whole thing and bring to light the true facts in order that people will retain some semblance of confidence in this organization that could be of tremendous benefit on the international scene.
Here is an agency that spends about $850 million a year, and there is no direct parliamentary control over it. According to reports the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated that he had no intention of bringing it under parliamentary control. So we see how control over government expenditures by parliament has been eroded, and is still being eroded. More than that, it is being supported by the government and by the Prime Minister personally when he refuses to have an inquiry into the various aspects of these expenditures. No wonder democracy in this country is suffering when this type of activity goes on and the government, first of all permits it, and secondly, tries to hide it by refusing an investigation! To carry out this activity, I suggest, is complete and utter incompetence; it is mismanagement of public money.
Two reasons can be found for this psychology of spend, spend, spend. One reason, and this is the most obvious and has been a concern for the opposition in parliament for years, is the intense rivalry between various government departments to increase their proportion of total government spending. What deputy minister or other departmental official wants his budget cut or frozen? He, to use the words of one writer, would be the object of scorn, whereas the hero in the whole process is the one who can boost his department's spending by a greater percentage than the federal total is increased.
Another reason, and one that may be less obvious but which nevertheless is well documented, is that the government is each year receiving an embarrassingly large amount of income from the taxpayers of the nation. In the first place the much discussed tax reform of 1970-1971 really contained a massive tax increase for which the people of this country have yet to be compensated. This really, according to an article in the Ottawa Journal of September 3, 1974, is the outgrowth of another intense rivalry, namely, the one between different levels of government for the tax dollar. It reads:
Rather than reduce the tax levels and thereby provide more tax room for the provinces and municipalities, the federal government finds ways to spend-though usually wastes it.
I could go into details on further expenditures by the present government that are completely irresponsible, but I do not think that there is any need to document this particular aspect of the problem any more today. This is one reason why I think that municipal property taxes, or some proportion thereof, should be made deductible on personal income tax. I hope the minister will consider that.
When I was speaking in the debate on housing yesterday I made reference to some other ways in which I believe the government could assist in the home ownership program. It is incomprehensible to find the government continually re-affirming its belief that each and every citizen of Canada has the right to decent and adequate housing, while all the time it continues to implement policies that destroy that capacity and keep people from owning their own homes.
In the second place the government induced inflation is bringing more and more taxpayers' money into its coffers than ever before. The one-year lag in the implementation of my leader's proposal for indexing personal incomes to offset the impact of inflation on personal income has resulted in what surely must be a surprising amount of income tax revenue for the Minister of Finance. I ask, just because it was an unexpected amount, whether that means that the government has a right to spend it? I ask whether the minister could not rebate the tax money which is received in that way?
The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) pointed out in the budget debate the fact that in his May, 1974, budget the Minister of Finance forecast a deficit of $450 million. Last September it was announced that there was a budgetary surplus of revenue amounting to $560 million, for a total of about $1 billion. To my mind this is an exercise which would not inspire public confidence in the Minister of Finance, or in the government. If the minister were the head of a business firm and made that kind of error, he would be out of a job very quickly. Rumours are that he is heading that way.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext: The old slide rule has a lot of rubber in it.
At least I could read it, Wally.

The minister is the head of a household. I ask him in all honesty and sincerity whether he would turn the books over to his wife if he had made this type of error in his family finances?
Again, just because there is a surplus in budgetary revenues, does that mean that the government must spend it indiscriminately, haphazardly, and without regard to sensible priorities?
The minister in this bill has proposed what he calls tax cuts from personal income tax. That again is complete and utter nonsense when you look at the minister's own figures. On the basis of the supposed reductions and the additional exemptions we should find the income tax yield for 1974-75 is lower than 1973-74. Even taking inflation into account, even taking new taxpayers and higher

January 31, 1975

numbers taken off the tax rolls into account, the total revenues from personal income tax should be lower. But what do we find? We find that the tax yield for 1974-75 will be 27 per cent higher than it was in 1973-74 simply because of an unjust and oppressive tax system, and inflation which the government does not even try to control.
The total tax revenues of the government will increase 32 per cent, by about $51 billion, on the basis of the tables of budgetary revenues introduced by the minister on November 18, 1974. Revenues from corporation income tax will increase, as will all revenues from all other sources, for a total of $5,730 billion in added government revenue.
Personal income tax alone will net the government an extra $2.1 billion next year, and the minister has the colossal nerve to talk about tax cuts. It seems that the more he cuts taxes, the higher they go. It does not seem to be logical or reasonable no matter how you look at it.
I would think, in view of all of this, that the minister should reconsider his proposals, give the Canadian taxpayer a break, and make the tax cut which he talks about mean something.
We find, when we look across the border, that President Ford has realized the necessity for this type of program, and I believe the minister referred to that when he was speaking the other day. I wish he would take it seriously as a challenge, and implement something of a similar nature here. Inflation is at such a rate now that a tax cut of $100, which the minister has been talking about, really is a loss for the taxpayer through a loss in purchasing power.
There are a couple of items in this budget which may help ease the burden somewhat. The $1,000 interest exemption provision is only fair, and has long been overdue. Previously if a person had to borrow money, he had to pay interest. This interest was tax deductible, but if he happened at some stage in the year to have money earn interest for him, that money was taxable. I suggest that this is unfair. It was even more unfair in relation to those who owned mortgages.
Some people pay out thousands of dollars each year on residential mortgages by way of interest payments. At least part of this should be deductible from personal income tax, but to date that has not been done. Yet if a person paying out all this money happened to earn a few dollars' interest on bonds or savings, then it is added on to his personal income and taxed. I suggested that this is oppressive in principle and in practice.
I suggest that the government's statement relative to tax policy is confusing and misleading. In effect it amounts to confiscation, and in application it is certainly inconsistent and discriminatory.
It has just been brought to my attention today that a very strange situation exists with respect to income tax and deductibility clauses. It was pointed out to me that commercials on the media urge that citizens take flying lessons and the cost can be listed as a tax deductible item. On the other hand, medical expenses can only be deducted on the basis of the proportion of expenditures above 3 per cent of one's income. How, in the name of common
Income Tax
sense, can these inconsistencies be perpetrated? One can take flying lessons and receive a deduction, yet when the taxpayer pays his medical and dental bills, he does not receive any deduction unless it goes beyond 3 per cent of his income, and then only the amount in excess of 3 per cent.
A further anomaly is found in the fact that if one qualifies and is in receipt of welfare benefits-and I am not implying that it should be otherwise-his medical expenses are taken care of; but if a person is in receipt of an income a little above that which qualifies him for welfare, he must pay his own medical, dental and other costs.
I have pleaded on behalf of those in the category usually referred to as the working poor, but so far nothing has been done to compensate them for their initiative either in the way of tax deductions or supplementary income.
I believe I mentioned before that I met with a group of single parents who were endeavouring, to the best of their ability, to get along without dependence on welfare benefits. They were working for a very low rate of pay. They were paying their own medical and dental bills, and they were finding it absolutely impossible to make ends meet. Could I obtain any help for them? No, not a cent. I suppose the government would rather have them quit their jobs and go on welfare so that it could support them wholly, rather than give them a little to help them over the hump and still retain what they believe is their integrity and their dignity.
In saying this I am not casting aspersions on those who are receiving welfare or other assistance because of incapacities of various kinds or inability to obtain work, but I am speaking on behalf of those who can find work but are not sufficiently well paid to enable them to live in dignity. I challenge the minister and the government, if they honestly care about this group of people, to do something to help. If they do not, a lot more of them are going to quit and become dependent on the public purse. I make a plea on their behalf. I trust the Minister of Finance, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) and other members of the government will give consideration to those who are desperately trying to make their own way in life.
My hon. friend, the member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro), mentioned the people who have been able to save for their declining years and now find, because of inflation and taxation, that their savings have been eroded. They wonder whether it paid them to try to provide for their retirement, and some feel it would have been better if they had spent as they earned. That way they would have received more from the public purse than they can get now. These are inconsistencies to which the Minister of Finance should direct his attention very quickly.
I suggest we should start all over again, Mr. Speaker. A voluminous tax reform bill was introduced in 1971, and now here comes Bill C-49 with 287 pages. I suppose that looks better. The so-called tax reform bill was not reform at all, but was a bill that raised taxes. In spite of all efforts to make it simple, it remained incomprehensible to the majority of Canadians. Even people competent in the tax

field had great difficulty analysing and explaining it. I suggest we start all over again and devise a tax structure that provides more equitable participation by all Canadians in the task of financing collectively what we individually cannot provide for ourselves.
Hear, hear!
The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay).

speakeroldname: Mr. G. H. Whittaker (Okanagan Boundary) moved:
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING VETERANS' OVERSEAS SERVICE
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to bringing in an amendment to the Old Age Security Act to ensure the Canadian veteran with overseas service that such service be counted for time in Canada for the purpose of the Old Age Security Act whether or not he has resided full-time after discharge in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on January 7, 1974, I received a copy of a letter written to one of my constituents by the regional director of old age security in Victoria. It reads as follows:
For our purpose we cannot consider you as physically present in Canada when we have confirmed that you were overseas with the Canadian armed forces from June 8, 1940 to March, 1946 and in addition left Canada again in November of 1946. The Old Age Security Act does not permit us to consider overseas service as physically present in Canada for old age security purposes.
When I read this letter I was outraged. Here is a man who has served his country. He joined the armed forces very soon after World War II broke out and was immedi-
January 31, 1975

ately sent overseas. That was not his choice. Now it seems he is not considered a Canadian citizen.
He came to Canada in the early 1920's, went overseas with the Canadian armed forces where he served for at least six years, and returned to Canada in 1946 for discharge. He spent six months in Canada, then went back to England where he pursued his occupation. For most of his time in England he worked for the Canadian government.
When he returned to Canada he found he did not qualify for the old age pension because the time he had spent overseas 'was counted as time when he had not been present in Canada. In other words when he went overseas it was determined that, for the purposes of the act, he could no longer be considered as a citizen resident in Canada and therefore could not qualify for the old age pension, even though he had served in the Canadian armed forces.
If I had done what he did-and I served in the Canadian armed forces but did not go overseas-I would, on returning to Canada, have been eligible for my old age pension. Yet this man, who had served in the Canadian armed forces, was told that the time he had spent in the service of his country outside his country did not count. That, really, is what prompted me to bring forward this motion.
I am against this type of discrimination which works to the detriment of people who served overseas in the armed forces. That is why I asked questions in the House of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde), and then brought forward a private member's motion and a private member's bill. The government has repeatedly said that it will act on this matter and bring forward an amendment to this act which will take care of my complaint.
This question was debated in the previous parliament, but nothing Was done. When the present session of the new parliament opened I immediately brought forward the same motion. I am beginning to wonder whether the promise previously made was hollow. My constituent and others similarly placed in Canada are being discriminated against in not being entitled to their old age pension. That being so I brought forward my motion again, and I wish to propose an amendment to it.
I hope the promise that something will be done to remedy this situation was not a hollow one. I hope it was not like the promise recently made by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson) to the effect that many people in Canada will benefit from $500 home ownership grants. It is now apparent that very few will qualify for such grants.
When this question was debated in the last parliament, the hon. member for Thunder Bay (Mr. Penner) spoke for 20 minutes. In his rambling speech he referred to what had happened as long ago as 1908. The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said that his speech touched on what had happened in pensions, almost since the day of his birth. But the hon. member for Thunder Bay did not deal with overseas service and time spent overseas in the service of this country counting as time spent in this country. The second speaker in the debate,
Old Age Security
who now is the Minister of State for Urban Affairs, referred to me as an apple picker or peach picker. Perhaps such wise observations led to his appointment as minister. But he did not touch on the roots of the problem.
Being concerned about this question, I have brought forward the motion moved this afternoon. I am pleased to learn that the minister will accept the motion if there is a slight amendment, to which I am more than willing to agree. I therefore wish to move an amendment.

I cannot commit the government, and the hon. member cannot blame me, as there is no way of knowing when the session will end. It could end on our next sitting day and a new session could begin immediately afterwards.
Let me explain the reasons behind the amendment. A person may qualify for the old age pension in one of three ways. He or she may:
(1)	have resided in Canada after the reaching the age of 18 for periods which total at least 40 years, or
(2)	have resided in Canada for the ten years immediately before approval of the application; or
(3)	have been present in Canada after reaching age 18 and prior to the ten years mentioned above for periods which equal, when totalled, at least three times the length of absences during the ten year period and have resided in Canada for at least one year immediately preceding the approval of the application.
It is with respect to this third requirement that the situation referred to by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) arises. I might say in passing that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) often criticizes my profession for the obscurity of the language, and I can tell him that there are a lot of lawyers who would like to see legislation put into better or less complicated English.
As the minister has stated on previous occasions, the old age security regulations provide that certain absences from Canada of a resident shall be deemed not to have interrupted that person's residence in Canada if certain prescribed conditions are met. These include absences while a person is employed or engaged by the United Nations, one of its specialized agencies, a Canadian firm or corporation, the federal government, as a member of the Canadian armed forces pursuant to and in connection with the requirements of his duty, as a missionary, or other similar employment or engagement.
However, the regulations do not provide that periods of absence under these circumstances may be deemed not to have interrupted that person's presence in Canada in determining his eligibility under the presence requirement. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) is of the opinion that such periods should be counted as presence in Canada, as he indicated some time

ago when the matter arose in connection with an application for old age security by a person who had been overseas in the Canadian army during World War II. In this case, the date on which he became eligible was set back because his period of overseas service could not be counted as presence in Canada.
The minister then sought advice from legal experts who determined that an amendment to the Old Age Security Act was required before a regulation could be made to deem absences of this kind as not interrupting presence in Canada. The point I am making is that the Act will have to be amended before regulations could be made giving effect to the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary.
In conclusion I might say that an investigation has revealed that the number of cases where a resident of Canada could not qualify for the pension on the normal date of eligibility because he was unable to count an absence from Canada while a member of the Canadian forces as presence in Canada, is very small and has occurred only in the context of extended periods of other absence from Canada. Although the number is small the government appreciates the difficulty which a delay in becoming eligible for the pension may cause the person concerned. If I might put my personal oar in, may I say I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. I hope this will be achieved this session.

Mr. Speaker, I commend the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) for having raised this issue in the last parliament and for having pressed it again in this first session of this parliament. I underscore the point made by the parliamentary secretary that this applies to a very few people; this particular constituent may go back to Britain to live and may not be able to vote for the hon. member or anyone else. However, it seems to me that parliament is at its best when it is doing things that are right regardless of the political effect they may have.
Both of those who have spoken have sought to explain what we are doing. Perhaps I might join the club and do it my way as well. As the parliamentary secretary has pointed out, there are certain basic ways in which one qualifies for old age security benefits. The standard way is simply to have been in Canada for ten years immediately preceding one's 65th birthday. There are, however, other arrangements for persons who do not meet this basic qualification. If they are not here for the ten years between the ages of 55 and 65, they can make up for any years that are missing by having been in Canada three times that number of years between the ages of 18 and age 55. In addition, of course, they must be here for the final year.
This appears to be a sensible arrangement and most people who ought to get a pension do meet these qualifications. The case the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary has produced is one which shows that even well-thought-out laws or regulations do not invariably cover all the points. The veteran to whom the hon. member has referred missed the capacity to produce the three times the number of years he has to produce, because for some of that time he was a Canadian serviceman residing in England.

I think it is proper that the proposed change should be made, and if the law officers say it requires an amendment to the act I am glad that such an amendment is to be made. Therefore, I commend not only the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary for raising the issue but I commend the government for its willingness to accept a private member's motion even though it was raised by a member on the opposition side of the House.
I notice that the parliamentary secretary, in doing what he was given to do officially, made the statement that the minister hoped to bring in the necessary amendment during the life of this parliament. As hon. members will realize, this parliament could last until 1979, and this is why I was particularly pleased to hear the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Cullen)-that is a pretty important post, and maybe he has some influence on the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde)-say it was his personal hope that it could be done this session.

I should be out of order, Mr. Speaker, if I tried to use this motion as an opportunity to make a speech calling for an increase in the amount of the pension and the lowering of the age of eligibility, though hon. members know this is on my mind. Nevertheless, I think it is in order to suggest that when the minister is considering an amendment to the act with respect to residence qualifications he should take a look at the other residence requirements in the legislation. There is one in particular, and the parliamentary secretary alluded to it this afternoon. I refer to the provision which affects persons leaving Canada before having reached the age of 65. Such a person can still get the pension if he has been in Canada for 40 years after the age of 18.
As a result of that there are individuals-I have had a case or two, and again we are talking about just a few cases, and they are persons away from Canada, but we are talking about what is fair-who were born in this country, have lived ih Canada for 57 years, but still do not get the pension because they have gone elsewhere.
On the other hand, I am proud of the fact that we have relaxed the residence requirements so that a person can come to Canada at the age of 55, live here for ten years, and get the pension. But I think there is an element of unfairness if someone can be here for only ten years and get the pension, whereas someone else who was born here, and who lived here for 57 years and 11 months, still does not get the pension. That is why I ask that all these residence requirements be looked at again.
Old Age Security
I am asking for something to be done in a field that has been amended several times. It has been done, if I may say so for the benefit of my hon. friend from Calgary, when parties on both sides have been in power. The length of time that one has to be in Canada has been reduced. Provision has been made for getting the pension after a certain number of years, even though a pensioner lives elsewhere. If these sort of changes have been made, I suggest that a further improvement can be made in respect to a number of elements in the residence requirements.
I commend the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary for having persisted in this matter, and I commend the government for agreeing to this proposition. I hope the bill that this motion calls for will be presented at an early date, and I am sure it will not take the House long to pass it.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to see you in the Chair; you have always presided over our deliberations so well. I should like the preceding speaker to know that Friday between the hour of four and five is the very peak of parliamentary attendance; it is one of my favourite days. There is such an intimate gathering of good people here that I hate to miss the Friday afternoon show. It is almost as agreeable as the late night show, another aspect of our parliamentary schedule that I like very much.
I want to begin by congratulating most heartily, as I did in the previous parliament, the initiator of this very fine piece of what I would describe as remedial legislation, which is what it amounts to. The first time that the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) came here, he noted an anomaly in the legislation. Indeed it was not an anomaly but in fact an outrage, a very grave injustice against certain people, and he has been persistent and assiduous in trying to correct it. I commend him for his leadership, and I commend the spokesman for the government for its response. I think even its amendment is an improvement.
I have noted that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) not long ago led a most prestigious group of solons and archons over to Westminster to discuss the ways of that ancient place. I would say that this afternoon demonstrates one way in which we can improve our proceedings, and that is by a more frequent attitude of acceptance on the part of the government toward the private members' hour. I think it is an extremely good attitude in the performance of parliament when a private member introduces a motion or public bill; there is nothing in the world to prevent the government from saying that it is a good idea, that it is a measure whereby service to the people may be improved or a piece of legislation may be improved. This should happen much more often.
I note that in another section of private members' business there stands a bill in the name of the hon. member for Windsor-Walkerville (Mr. MacGuigan) regarding heritage day. I also had a bill with reference to a holiday, and I would have been glad to withdraw mine in favour of his. Had that been done before Christmas we might have been able to have a holiday on heritage day this year, a measure which would have emanated from this particular hour in our proceedings. So I commend the government

I think the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary has shown he is a good legislator, because there are so many aspects of our legislation, and indeed of the regulations built thereon, which are ridiculous. I have told the House before about a constituent of mine who wanted to qualify for the residence period for purposes of old age security. He went to the office of the Department of National Health and Welfare and they said to him: "Sir, if you come back in 33 and one-third years we can qualify you." Through my intervention we got the period down to nine years, but at 88 he was not even sure that would help very much.
As I say, there are many other items we could look at, but the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary must be

May I tell the learned and venerable hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that I am sure that when the government has all the details ready and wants to bring forward the amending bill, there will be no disposition to do otherwise than to proceed with expedition so that a little more justice will be extended to a few more of our people.
